subject: Civil Engineering
title: Caissons: Building Underwater
description: A quick, practical guide to Caissons: Building Underwater.

hook.text: How do you dig a foundation at the bottom of a river? You send a box down.

buildup.text: A caisson is a watertight chamber sunk to the riverbed. Workers excavate inside.

discovery.text: Pneumatic caissons use compressed air to keep water out — workers breathe pressurized air.

twist.text: Rapid decompression caused 'the bends' — joint pain, paralysis, even death.

climax.text: Modern caissons use robotic excavation — no workers in pressurized chambers.

punchline.text: Sinking a box to bedrock is still the best way to start underwater.

quiz.question: What medical condition affected workers in pneumatic caissons?
options: Decompression sickness (the bends) from rapid pressure changes
Hearing loss from underwater noise levels

details.summary: Caissons are large, pre-fabricated structural boxes or cylinders sunk through water and soft soil to provide foundations for bridges, ports, and other waterfront structures. Open caissons sink under their own weight while soil is excavated from inside.
details.whyItMatters: Caissons provide massive foundations for the world's longest bridges and deepest waterfront structures in conditions where no other foundation method is feasible.
takeaways: Open caissons sink by self-weight as soil is excavated from inside the chamber
Pneumatic caissons use compressed air to exclude water during deep excavation
Modern deep caissons can reach depths exceeding 60 meters below water level

faq.question: What are the health hazards of working in pneumatic caissons?
faq.answer: Workers in compressed air caissons risk decompression sickness, known as the bends, if they ascend too quickly. Nitrogen dissolves in blood under high pressure and forms dangerous bubbles during rapid decompression.

faq.question: How is soil removed from inside a sinking caisson?
faq.answer: In open caissons, clamshell buckets or airlift systems remove soil through the water inside the caisson. In pneumatic caissons, workers excavate in a compressed-air chamber at the bottom while excavated soil is lifted through airlocks.
